accuracy.evidence: Checked against the National Curriculum in England English Appendix 1 (Year 1 spelling): vowel digraphs ai, oi, ay, oy, ee, ea, oa, oe, oo are listed, with the note that ai and oi are virtually never used at the end of English words while ay and oy are used there; CCSS RF.1.3.c (vowel team conventions for long vowel sounds). The lab only uses words that follow the taught rule (play, boy, train, soil) and the adult text names exceptions to watch for (ea in head and bread).

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the four errors teachers see most in Year 1: sounding every letter (b-o-a-t; the letters tag and the join step's wrong-pair feedback), spelling final ai as in plai (aiend tag, Middle or end step), reading every oo as long (long tag, Moon or book sort with foot, look, good), and assuming one sound has only one spelling (Sound houses with ee/ea, ai/ay, oa/oe; mix and other tags).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagvowel is the only lab where children draw a line between adjacent letter tiles to merge them and the sound buttons switch from two dots to one bar; flagdgraph works on consonant pairs with magnets and a sound counter, while this lab adds phoneme frames that reject a single o for oo, a position rule gap for ai/ay and oi/oy, a long/short oo sort and three sound houses.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each step isolates one idea a Year 1 child needs: two letters can be one grapheme (join), sounds not letters fill the frame (coin needs 3 boxes), position decides ai versus ay, one grapheme can carry two phonemes (oo), and one phoneme can have two graphemes (houses). Wrong moves explain why, e.g. placing ea in seed says ea can make that sound but seed is spelt with ee.

predictions.evidence: Four predictions ask the child to commit before acting, and each has a tempting wrong option: 4 sounds for rain (one per letter), 4 boxes for coin, ai at the end like plai, and moon and book sharing a sound. The reveal after each step confirms or corrects the guess with the words they just built.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Five rotating questions with tagged distractors; every wrong answer gets its own reason, for instance choosing oy for coin explains that oy usually goes at the end like boy, and choosing moon for the book sound explains that moon has the long oo while book and foot share the short one. Streak count rewards repeats without blocking progress.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use short sentences and words a 5 year old hears in phonics lessons (two letters, one sound; middle; end; long; short) with worked examples r-ai-n, t-r-ee, b-oa-t. Adult paragraphs carry the exact terms grapheme, phoneme, digraph, vowel digraph, sound buttons and phoneme frame, and cite NC Year 1 and RF.1.3.c.

no_filler.evidence: Every paragraph adds something new: the idea, the sound count, the position rule, the oo split, then curriculum, terminology, common mistakes with the ea caution, and a lab walkthrough. Practice and mastery items each test a different skill (count sounds, frame boxes, position spelling, oo sound, shared spellings).

mobile.evidence: Walked on iPhone 13 light and dark: letter tiles scale to fit four letters with room for + hooks, tray tiles and sound houses fit across 390px, all text is at least 12px and wraps, and the young class gives big button twins for every drag (join pairs, tiles, ai/ay, moon/book, houses).

accessibility.evidence: Every action has a labelled button twin (aria-label such as Join a and i, Put oi in the next box, Post it to the ee house); the canvas aria-label and live status speak each result; axe passed in both themes; reduced motion shortens timers; colours come from the theme palette so contrast holds in light and dark.

sources: National Curriculum in England: English programmes of study, Year 1 Word Reading and English Appendix 1 Spelling (DfE, 2013)
Common Core State Standards for English Language Arts, Reading Foundational Skills RF.1.3.c
Letters and Sounds: Principles and Practice of High Quality Phonics (DfES, 2007), Phase 3 and Phase 5
